title: Elliott A. Brooks Carvings
summary: Beginning in 1933, Elliott Alvah Brooks carved figures into shoreline boulders in Orient. The carvings, later called Bear Rock Studio, were cataloged as a memorial to Poquatuck people. Brooks was a non-Native artist and collector, so the place also raises questions about who interprets Indigenous history and how Native belongings were collected during the twentieth century.
why_this_matters: The carvings preserve a local memory of Poquatuck people while showing the limits of memorials created through a non-Native collector's viewpoint. Their history invites a fuller account centered on Indigenous presence rather than disappearance.
history_content: Brooks carved approximately twenty-five figures into boulders along the Long Island Sound shore. The Smithsonian catalog identifies the work as Poquatuck and Montauk Indians Memorial Carvings. Local reporting also describes Brooks's collecting of Native belongings. Together, these histories distinguish an act of memorialization from the harmful treatment of Indigenous heritage as collectible material.
preservation_content: Oysterponds Historical Society photographed and documented the carvings as erosion and changing shoreline conditions threatened them. The carvings remain on a fragile shore where access, ownership, and preservation require care.
